blocks.text: Nine passages of the Prophets which some interpreters refer to sparrows, for the most part rather uncertain. I. Levit. XIV. passim. II. Iob. XL, 24. III. Psal. X, 1. IV. Psal. LXXXIV, 4. V. Psal. CII, 8. VI. Psal. CIV, 16. VII. Psal. CXXIV, 7. VIII. Eccles. XII, 4. IX. Thren. III, 52.
Interpreters do not sufficiently agree in which passages of Scripture צפור tsippor is taken for the sparrow. For of the nine passages that are adduced, most are very doubtful.

I. The first is Levit. XIV., at the beginning of the chapter and at the end, where it treats of two צפורים tsipporim, by which, one being killed and the other released, the leper was purified, and also a house infected with leprosy. Most hold that the tsipporim there are sparrows, as Jerome, Pagninus, Arias, the Genevans and others render it. But that birds in general are meant will be clear to anyone who reads attentively verse four: And let him that is to be cleansed take שתי צפורים חיות טהרות, two living clean tsipporim. This does not fit the sparrow, whether it is held to have been clean or unclean. For it could not be called clean if by the Law it was unclean. Conversely, if it was clean, the Law would have commanded in vain that clean sparrows be taken, since there were no unclean ones. Nowhere is it commanded that clean doves [col. 151] or turtledoves be offered, because all were clean. It appears, therefore, that צפורים tsipporim there are birds in general; and since some of these were clean and others unclean, God commands that clean ones be taken, for instance doves or turtledoves, which are called הצפור in Gen. XV, 10., or any others, provided they are clean and permitted as food according to the law of Deut. XIV, 11. כל צפור טהרה תאכלו, Every clean tsippor you shall eat. Thus, as we showed above, some understand hens here too, and the Greek ὀρνίθια [ornithia] can be referred to this. Nor do the Hebrews specify a species, provided they are צפרים דרור טהורות, free and clean birds. On the rite of this purification Maimonides has much that is notable in the treatise On Leprosy, chapter 11, which does not belong here.

II. The second passage is in the description of the Leviathan, Iob. XL, 24. (var. 29.), and in Hebrew it reads thus: Will you play with him כצפור, as with a tsippor? And will you bind him for your girls? And in the Greek version: Παίξῃ δὲ ἐν αὐτῷ ὥσπερ ὀρνέῳ; ἢ δήσεις αὐτὸν ὥσπερ [col. 152] στρουθίον παιδίῳ; [Paixē de en autō hōsper orneō; ē dēseis auton hōsper strouthion paidiō?] Will you play with him as with a bird? and will you bind him like a sparrow for a child? And in the Arabic: هل تضحك عليه مثل العصفور [hal taḍḥaku ʿalayhi mithla al-ʿuṣfūr] Will you play with him as with a sparrow, etc. Those who pursue mysteries refer this to the devil, as though through baptism and conversion he were handed over to us bound, [II, 728] like a little sparrow to a child. Origen, of the faithful man: Ὅ γε δράκων αὐτῷ ὥσπερ στρουθίον παραδέδοται παιδίῳ· [Ho ge drakōn autō hōsper strouthion paradedotai paidiō] The dragon has been handed over to him as a sparrow to a child. And shortly after: Τῇ χάριτι τοῦ Κυρίου, ὡς στρουθίον ὑποχείριον, ὁ Σατανᾶς δεδεμένος γεγένηται τοῖς νηπίοις, καὶ θηλάζουσιν, ὧν ἐκ στόματος κατηρτίσατο αἶνον ὁ Θεός· [Tē chariti tou Kyriou, hōs strouthion hypocheirion, ho Satanas dedemenos gegenētai tois nēpiois, kai thēlazousin, hōn ek stomatos katērtisato ainon ho Theos] By the grace of the Lord, like a tame sparrow, Satan has been bound for children and sucklings, out of whose mouth God has perfected his praise. Chrysostom: Δήσας τὸν ἐχθρὸν ὁ Κύριος ἡμῶν δέδωκε καταπαίζειν αὐτοῦ, ὡς στρουθίου, τοῖς στραφεῖσι, καὶ γενομένοις ὡς τὰ παιδία. [Dēsas ton echthron ho Kyrios hēmōn dedōke katapaizein autou, hōs strouthiou, tois strapheisi, kai genomenois hōs ta paidia.] To those who have been converted and have become as infants, our Lord has handed over the adversary, bound, to be mocked like a sparrow. Alluding to this, the author of the life of Pachomius, chapter 49, attributes these words to the devils: Since the wonderful incarnation of Christ took place on earth, we have begun to exist wholly without strength; so that we are mocked like sparrows by those who believe in his name. Leaving these aside, we ask only whether the Hebrew is well rendered: Will you play with him as with a sparrow? and will you bind him for your young ones? That a mention of the sparrow is fitting here is suggested by that very well-known line of Catullus,
Sparrow, darling of my girl, with whom she is wont to play, whom to hold in her lap, to whom, as it seeks it, to give her fingertip and to provoke its sharp bites.

Hence Arnobius, book 7: as little boys (to spare their feelings and keep from crying) are given little sparrows, poplar toys, loaves, with which they can divert themselves. And an Arab poet, whom Ibno Rasik cites in the book entitled غرايب [gharāyib] garaibo, that is, Curiosities:
كعصفورة في كف طفل يسوخها * حياض الردي والطفل يلهو ويلعب * [ka-ʿuṣfūratin fī kaffi ṭiflin yasūkhuhā * ḥiyāḍa al-radī wa-l-ṭiflu yalhū wa-yalʿabu *]

Like a hen sparrow in a boy's hand, which he plunges into the evil troughs while he jests and plays. Yet in Job there is no need to understand the sparrow precisely, since there is no lack of other birds with which boys and girls are equally amused. Plautus in the Captivi, Act 5:
— — as jackdaws, or ducks, or quails are given to patrician boys to play with.
